name: Pointe-à-Pitre Pôle Caraïbes
before:
Guadeloupe's main airport, and the second busiest in the Lesser Antilles after Aruba. It handled close to 2.5 million passengers in 2019, ahead of Barbados.

It sits in Abymes, only 2.4 km from Pointe-a-Pitre, and works from two interconnected terminals. The runway is longer than the island's traffic suggests at 3,125 metres, enough to take an A380 without difficulty. One of the A380 prototypes spent two days here in January 2006.

Air Caraibes uses it as its main hub, and Air France keeps two A320s based on the island for regional flying, so connections around the archipelago are better than at most Caribbean gateways. It is the largest of six airports across Guadeloupe.

The airport now carries the name of Maryse Conde, though it is still widely listed as Pointe-a-Pitre or Pole Caraibes, so expect to see all three on schedules.
after:
Guadeloupe's main airport. It handled more than 2.1 million passengers in 2025, still short of the nearly 2.5 million of 2019.

The airport sits in Abymes, just north of Pointe-à-Pitre, and has two terminals, the smaller T2 serving regional flights. Its runway is about 3,500 metres long, and an A380 made a technical stop here in January 2006.

Air Caraïbes has its main base here, and both it and Air France fly to Paris and around the region. Regional links were hit when Air Antilles stopped flying at the end of 2025, so check onward connections before booking.

It now carries the name Guadeloupe Maryse Condé, but the older names Pointe-à-Pitre Le Raizet and Pôle Caraïbes are still in use, so expect to see all three.

claims.claim: more than 2.1 million passengers in 2025
claims.inAfter: It handled more than 2.1 million passengers in 2025
claims.note: Was 'close to 2.5 million passengers in 2019'. UAF gives 2,193,878 for 2025 including transit, of which 2,146,585 local passengers; Eurostat, which counts passengers carried without transit, gives 2,146,387. Both are above 2.1 million, so the text says that (as for Bergen). The drafting note said Eurostat does not cover the airport; it does (FR_TFFR). The operator's own 2025 total could not be found: its press page lists only four releases (the latest, January and March 2026 traffic, give monthly figures), and its annual activity reports stop at 2024.

sources.quote: passengers carried in 2025: 2,146,387

claims.claim: still short of the nearly 2.5 million of 2019
claims.inAfter: still short of the nearly 2.5 million of 2019
claims.note: Keeps the old 2019 figure as the benchmark: 2,488,782 in both sources, and 11.8 per cent above 2025 on UAF's figures.

sources.quote: In 2019, the airport handled 2,488,782 passengers

claims.claim: in Abymes, just north of Pointe-à-Pitre
claims.inAfter: The airport sits in Abymes, just north of Pointe-à-Pitre
claims.note: Was 'only 2.4 km from Pointe-a-Pitre'. Coordinates give 3.2 km at 3 degrees (north) from the GeoNames centre; 2.4 km is a ratio of 0.75, below the tolerance, and the one written source for it is Wikipedia (the current eAIP page could not be fetched: two URL forms answered 404). The operator's legal notice gives its address as Morne Mamiel, 97139 Abymes.

claims.claim: regional links hit when Air Antilles stopped flying at the end of 2025
claims.inAfter: Regional links were hit when Air Antilles stopped flying at the end of 2025
claims.note: Replaces 'so connections around the archipelago are better than at most Caribbean gateways', a comparison with no second source that the collapse of Air Antilles has overtaken. The operator's release of 13 February 2026 dates the stop to 8 December (necessarily December 2025) and blames it for traffic to the northern islands falling 14.6 per cent in January 2026; its April release reports a 20.3 per cent fall in March. UAF's 2025 report says the liquidation of Air Antilles has durably affected air service in the area.

quote: COMMUNIQUÉ DE PRESSE Les Abymes, le 13 février 2026
une offre en recul du fait de l'arrêt des vols d'Air Antilles depuis le 8 décembre
Le faisceau « Îles du Nord » est en recul de -14,6 % avec 12 189 passagers, contre 14 265 en janvier 2025, en raison essentiellement de la suspension des opérations d'Air Antilles.
Aux Antilles, le trafic reste en baisse de 7,5 % par rapport à 2019, malgré une légère reprise en 2025 (+3,2 %).
Cette évolution demeure fortement pénalisée par la liquidation d'Air Antilles et des difficultés des croisières tête

sources.quote: Cependant, les faisceaux concernés par l'arrêt des vols d'Air Antilles subissent comme anticipé une baisse de trafic.
